fee.rule: 2026 Final QAP: developer fees up to $24,000 per unit for new construction (28.5% of PDC line item 4 for rehabilitation). Raised from $23,000 (2025 QAP) and $22,500 (2024 QAP).
fee.basis: Per unit (not a percent of cost).
fee.dollarCap: No separate per-project dollar cap on the fee was found. The per-project 9% credit award is capped at $1,500,000, which limits fundable cost.
fee.quote: "(a) Developer fees shall be up to $24,000 per unit for new construction projects and twenty-eight point five percent (28.5%) of PDC line item 4 for rehabilitation projects" (search-engine excerpt of the 2026 Final QAP; the first-draft revisions memo says "the per unit developer fee for new construction projects has been increased to $24,000", up from $23,000 in the 2025 QAP).

maxFeasibleUnits.evidence: Unit cap in the 2026 Final QAP (same in 2024 and 2025): "New construction 9% Tax Credit projects may not exceed the following: Metro Region - one hundred and twenty (120) units; Central, East, and West Regions - eighty-four (84) units." A 101-120 unit 9% new-construction deal is only possible in the Metro Region. The QAP also says "The maximum award to any one project will be $1,500,000." No specific 101+ unit 9% award in 2021-2025 was identified.

sponsorPath.evidence: 2026 Final QAP development-experience threshold (search excerpt): at least one Principal must have developed, operated and maintained in compliance either "one (1) 9% Tax Credit project in North Carolina or six (6) separate 9% Tax Credit projects totaling in excess of 200 units" (placed-in-service window applies; exact dates not confirmed). So an experienced out-of-state developer can qualify directly with six 9% deals anywhere, or by adding a Principal with one NC 9% deal. Developers commented that this sets "too high a bar for out of state experience" (Lincoln Avenue Communities). Evanston/Chicago-area Brinshore commented on the 2026 QAP jointly with a NC housing authority (RHA), which shows the partner route in use.

financingPath.evidence: Annual competitive 9% round with geographic regions; the Metro Region allows the largest (120-unit) projects, and each county's initial maximum award is "based on its percent share of the Metro region". 2025 round: about $31.5M of credits, 9% awards covering 1,503 units, about 262 of them preservation and the rest new construction; NCHFA's impact report lists 110 preliminary applications and 31 9% awards. NCHFA said every new-construction award in 2025 needed gap financing such as WHLP. Credits are available but heavily oversubscribed.

9%.nextDeadline: Not found. The 2027 QAP and its preliminary-application date were not located; NC preliminary 9% applications are normally due early in the year (the City of Raleigh's 2026 NOFA references a May 15, 2026 NCHFA full-application deadline for the 2026 cycle).

access.evidence: Direct path if DL3 has six 9% deals over 200 units in total (anywhere); otherwise add an NC-experienced Principal. Barriers: about 110 preliminary applications for 31 awards in 2025, a $1.5M per-project credit cap, a 120-unit cap even in the Metro Region, and county-share limits within the Metro Region.

urban.evidence: Charlotte/Mecklenburg has a documented shortage of 44,572 rental units for households under 50% AMI, and more than 77% of 2015 low-cost stock has been lost (county report via WFAE). But a 120-unit 9% deal with at most $1.5M of annual credit cannot cover a $40M budget without large local gap funds; NCHFA said every 2025 new-construction award needed gap financing. Local governments committed over $28M to 9% projects in 2024 (UNC SOG). No rent, cost or vacancy data was found.

execution.evidence: No local-office rule was found. Charlotte is roughly a 2-hour direct flight from Chicago (general knowledge, not sourced). Partner route via an NC-experienced Principal exists. A Chicago-area peer (Brinshore) is active in NC with a housing authority partner.

fee.rule: The 2026 QAP governs both 9% and tax-exempt bond / 4% applications; its developer-fee clause is up to $24,000 per unit for new construction. No separate, higher 4% fee rule was found. Developer comments on the draft asked NCHFA to raise the fee "at least for projects financed using 4% LIHTCs and TEBs" (suggesting at least $26,000 per unit) and said "many states in the region have higher developer fees for 4% transactions"; adoption was not confirmed.
fee.basis: Per unit (assumed to apply to bond deals; not confirmed in text).
fee.arithmetic: 120 units x $24,000 = $2,880,000, which is 7.2% of the $40,000,000 TDC. If a separate 4% rule exists it was not found.
fee.quote: "(a) Developer fees shall be up to $24,000 per unit for new construction projects and twenty-eight point five percent (28.5%) of PDC line item 4 for rehabilitation projects" (search-engine excerpt of the 2026 Final QAP; the first-draft revisions memo says "the per unit developer fee for new construction projects has been increased to $24,000", up from $23,000 in the 2025 QAP). Comment on the draft: "at least for projects financed using 4% LIHTCs and TEBs" (Lincoln Avenue Communities letter).

maxFeasibleUnits.evidence: Central at Old Concord, 5709 N Tryon St, Charlotte: 200-unit new-construction family project with NCHFA 4% credits and tax-exempt bonds, $28.4M of bonds issued by INLIVIAN, and more than $4M of City of Charlotte Housing Trust Fund money; listed with a 2023 year (Novogradac NC LIHTC property table) and under construction with completion expected summer 2027. The 120/84-unit caps apply only to 9% new construction.

sponsorPath.evidence: The development-experience text found is written for 9% projects; no 4%-specific experience rule or bar was found. No rule found that bars out-of-state sponsors from bond deals. Out-of-state developers such as The Annex Group (Indianapolis) and Dominium (Minneapolis) have done large Charlotte 4% deals, which suggests access in practice, but that is not a written QAP path.

financingPath.evidence: North Carolina's 2026 private activity bond cap is listed at $1,491,213,240 with a first-come, first-served process, preliminary deadline 10/1/26 and full deadline 1/15/27 (Novogradac table, via search excerpt). The 2026 QAP Appendix M implements the drop from the 50% to the 25% test, letting applicants request bond cap for the greater of 30% of aggregate basis or maximum supportable debt, which stretches the cap. The QAP sets a bond-cap priority order (public housing revitalization, then rehab of rent-restricted housing, then rehab of market-rate) where new construction is not first. No evidence of a multi-year waitlist was found. 2024 awards (credits and bonds) covered 50 projects, about $1.1B of development.

4%.nextDeadline: Bond cap: preliminary application deadline 10/1/26 (passed) and full application deadline 1/15/27, per the Novogradac 2026 state bond caps table (search excerpt, not verified on NCHFA).

access.evidence: No unit cap, and no 4%-specific experience bar found. Bond cap is large ($1.49B) and stretched by the 25% test, but new construction is not first in the bond-cap priority order and the 4% developer fee (assumed $24,000/unit) is low, so the 10%-of-TDC fee goal is not met.

urban.evidence: A 200-unit Charlotte 4% new-construction deal (Central at Old Concord) is under way with local bonds and Housing Trust Fund gap money. Shortage of 44,572 rental units under 50% AMI in Mecklenburg. The region added a record 19,754 apartments in the year to 2025 Q3 (UNC Charlotte), a lease-up competition risk. No rent, tax or insurance data was found for a downside case.

execution.evidence: No local-presence rule found; Charlotte is reachable by direct flight from Chicago (general knowledge). Out-of-state firms (Annex Group, Dominium) execute Charlotte 4% deals. Bond deals carry larger construction guarantees.

venture.market: Charlotte: Beatties Ford Road / Rozzelles Ferry Road Corridor of Opportunity (west of Uptown)

historicSuccess.evidence: A long-established west-side corridor that the city calls one of six "Corridors of Opportunity"; WFAE describes these corridors as "long neglected". City has completed Beatties Ford sidewalks and a bike boulevard, with intersection work in progress. No sourced data on past commercial vibrancy or transit ridership was found.

anchorInstitutions.evidence: The Park Church dedicated a 30-acre site on Beatties Ford Road for mixed-use affordable housing (including 125 multifamily units and senior housing), rezoned by City Council. Universities or hospitals investing in the corridor were not confirmed in sources found.

availableProperty.evidence: 30-acre Park Church site rezoned for affordable mixed use; the city is pursuing strategic land acquisitions in underserved areas. No specific vacant parcel sized for 100+ LIHTC units was confirmed.

emergingMomentum.evidence: Since 2020 the city has used housing bonds to fund nearly 2,400 affordable multifamily units in the Corridors (2022 annual report). Voters approved a $100M housing bond in 2024; a $125M bond was on the Nov. 2026 ballot (result not found).

localLeadership.evidence: City Council's Corridors of Opportunity program targets Beatties Ford/Rozzelles Ferry with housing, jobs, transportation and safety work; a city Housing Trust Fund ($34.3M cited in 2022 report) plus successive housing bonds ($50M 2020, $50M 2022, $100M 2024) provide gap funds; Mecklenburg County also funds affordable housing.

notes: nchfa.com, nchfa-live.agaric.com and housingonline.com could not be reached from this session (network block), so all NCHFA rules come from search-engine excerpts; ruleVerified is false. Fee: $24,000/unit new construction in the 2026 Final QAP gives $2.88M (7.2% of TDC) for both pathways; it was NOT confirmed whether bond/4% deals have a separate fee rule (commenters asked for one). The 2027 QAP (if adopted) was not found; its fee may differ. 9%: unit cap 120 (Metro) / 84 (other regions), $1.5M max credit per project. Experience rule: one NC 9% deal or six 9% deals over 200 units; placed-in-service dates not confirmed. Award counts: 2025 had 110 preliminary applications and 31 9% awards (NCHFA impact report); 2022 had 127 preliminary 9% applications; new-construction and over-100-unit counts were not found for any year, and 2021/2023 data were not found. 9% oversubscription by credits was not found (about 3.5 applications per award in 2025 is a rough proxy, not credits). 4% bond cap figure and deadlines come from a Novogradac table excerpt. Central at Old Concord's '2023' year is from a property table and may not be the award year; sponsor listed as Shelter Investments Development Corporation in an NCHFA listing vs. The Annex Group in press. Venture: Johnson C. Smith University and transit (Gold Line) links were not confirmed by sources. No Charlotte rent/vacancy/insurance data found.
